mission1.title: Get Out of Your Own Head
mission1.briefing_text: Before we look at business ideas, we need to focus on you. We're going to break out of the overthinking loop and build the habits you need to actually stick with this in the real world.

prerequisites.item: Commit to finding at least 3 hours a week.
prerequisites.promptRawText: The user is trying to find 3 hours a week while working full-time. Give them a practical strategy to protect three 60-minute blocks without burning out.

prerequisites.item: A reliable computer and a decent internet connection
Willingness to be completely honest with yourself and the system
prerequisites.promptRawText: The user is nervous about sharing their ideas. Remind them that starting matters more than keeping secrets, and hiding an idea just keeps them isolated.

quest1.title: Your Fresh Start
quest1.subtitle: Get real about why you are here, face your roadblocks, and introduce yourself.
quest1.description: Every great journey begins exactly where you are standing right now. Before we look at business ideas, let's nail down what is driving you to build, map out the real-world boundaries you are working around, and introduce yourself to your fellow founders.
quest1.persona_prompt: You are a grounded advisor and a supportive friend. Review user motivations and roadblocks. Call out vague answers kindly, and help them turn big dreams into everyday actions.

tasks.title: Why do you want to start a business?
tasks.description: Let's be totally honest. Building a business takes serious energy, and vague goals fade the moment life gets busy. What is the actual change you want to make in your life?

tasks.title: Be realistic about your schedule and roadblocks
tasks.description: Let's get real about your schedule and the roadblocks you are working around. This is about being honest with yourself so you can actually make progress.

tasks.title: Introduce yourself to the community
tasks.description: You're not in this alone. Put a face to the name, write a brief bio, and share your links so other people here can see what you're up to.

quest2.title: Learn to ask
quest2.subtitle: When you ask you might just get what you want!
quest2.description: The power of asking lies in its ability to unlock new possibilities, break down social barriers, and accelerate personal and professional growth. By overcoming the fear of rejection, you open yourself to feedback, better opportunities, and deeper connections with others
quest2.persona_prompt: You are a helpful copy editor. Review message drafts. Highlight hesitant filler words like 'just checking in' or 'sorry to bother you', and suggest more confident alternatives.

tasks.title: Element of a good ask
tasks.description: Lets practice few asks before you approach people in the real world.

tasks.title: Get your cheer squad
tasks.description: Ask people you know to be part of your journey. This could be a friend, a mentor, or a family member. Ask them to give you feedback on your idea, or just to be a cheerleader for your progress.

ai_config.reflection_prompt: Now that you've hit send, did the reality of doing it feel lighter than the anxiety you had beforehand?

tasks.title: Build your presence
tasks.description: Having a digital presence is important for building credibility and trust. It also helps you to be found by people who are interested in your work. Let's make sure you have a basic digital presence set up.

recommendations.title: Ways to build a digital presence

quest3.title: Get Used to Hearing No
quest3.subtitle: Collect a few real-world rejections and see that they won't kill you.
quest3.description: Hearing 'no' stings at first—that's normal. But here's the thing: it's not about you. It's just feedback. This module is a safe space to practice taking small knocks so you can see they don't actually hurt. By the end, you'll have proof that rejection is just information, not a verdict.
quest3.persona_prompt: You are an encouraging coach. The user is logging rejections. Reframe their entries as clean user feedback rather than personal setbacks.

tasks.title: Log 3 minor rejections this week
tasks.description: Here's a small experiment: go ask for something small that you expect to be turned down for. Maybe ask a cafe for a discount, or request a favor from someone you don't know well. The goal isn't to get a 'yes'—it's to collect a 'no' on purpose. When it happens, take a breath. Notice that you're okay. That's the whole point.

recommendations.title: Your First No Is the Hardest
Post your experience to the community board

ai_config.reflection_prompt: Now that you've done it—did the rejection actually hurt? Or did it just feel a little awkward and then pass? Write down what happened, how you felt, and what you noticed. This is your proof that you can handle more than you think.

tasks.title: See how your peers are doing
tasks.description: Open the community feed. Scroll through what others have posted. You'll see the same awkward moments, the same small rejections, the same 'I survived that' energy. This is your reminder that you're in good company.

mission2.title: Find Problems Worth Solving
mission2.briefing_text: Before you build anything, you need to find a problem worth solving. We're going to start with what you know best—your own frustrations—and gradually expand outward. By the end of this mission, you'll have a real opportunity you can turn into a business.

prerequisites.item: Your observation journal (PDF or physical notebook)
prerequisites.promptRawText: You've got your observation journal ready. This is your tool for capturing frustrations and annoyances in real life. Keep it with you—you'll be using it a lot in this mission.

prerequisites.item: Willingness to talk to people about their problems
prerequisites.promptRawText: You'll need to have real conversations with people—friends, colleagues, even strangers. This isn't about selling. It's about listening. Remind yourself: you're doing research, not pitching.
Finding a good problem takes time. You might feel like you're not making progress. That's normal. Trust the process—every observation is data.

quest1.title: Your Own Frustrations
quest1.subtitle: Start with what you know best—your own life
quest1.description: The best problems to solve are often the ones you experience yourself. You understand them intimately. You know the pain points. You're the expert. In this quest, we're going to mine your own frustrations and skills for business opportunities.
quest1.persona_prompt: You are a patient guide helping the user notice patterns in their own frustrations. Ask gentle questions that help them see their problems more clearly. Never dismiss their experiences. Help them connect dots.

tasks.title: Collect your frustrations and annoyances
tasks.description: For the next 7 days, keep your observation journal with you. Every time something frustrates you, annoys you, or makes you think 'there has to be a better way'—write it down. Don't judge it. Just collect. Aim for at least 10 entries. Notice patterns. What comes up again and again?

recommendations.title: How to Spot Hidden Opportunities in Your Frustrations
recommendations.subtitle: 5 min read

ai_config.reflection_prompt: After a week of observing, what patterns have you noticed? What are you most excited to explore further?

observation_config.briefing_text: For the next 7 days, keep your observation journal with you. guide_questions: What made you think 'I wish there was a better way'?
What did you spend too much time on?

What made you say 'that's just how it is'?

tasks.title: What are you better at than most people?
tasks.description: Now let's look at your skills. What do you do better than most people you know? This could be anything—cooking, organizing, explaining, fixing things, making people feel comfortable. Ask 3 people who know you well: 'What am I unusually good at?' And ask yourself: 'Would people pay me to do this for them?'

recommendations.title: How to Turn Your Skills Into a Business
recommendations.subtitle: 4 min read

ai_config.reflection_prompt: What did people say you're good at? Did any of their answers surprise you? How might your skills connect to the frustrations you observed?

What do you do that feels effortless to you but hard for others?

tasks.title: Enter your best opportunities
tasks.description: Open your observation journal. Pick the 3-5 frustrations that felt most real, most frequent, or most interesting. Also look at your skill reflections. Where do your skills and frustrations intersect? Enter them into the system as opportunities—these are the raw materials for your business.

recommendations.title: How to Write a Clear Problem Statement

metadata_config.source_context: Look at your frustration journal. Pick the 3-5 frustrations that felt most real, most frequent, or most interesting. Also look at your skill reflections. Where do your skills and frustrations intersect? Enter them as opportunities.

quest2.title: People in Your Circle
quest2.subtitle: The problems of people you know are the problems you understand best
quest2.description: Now we're expanding outward. The people you know—friends, family, colleagues, classmates—have problems too. And because you know them, you can observe their frustrations firsthand. This is research you can do without leaving your comfort zone.
quest2.persona_prompt: You are a curious researcher helping the user observe problems in their social circles. Encourage them to be good listeners. Help them distinguish between minor annoyances and real problems. Remind them: they're doing research, not pitching.

tasks.title: Observe the problems of people around you
tasks.description: Pick 3 people in your life. Could be a friend, a colleague, a family member, someone at your gym. Over the next week, observe them. What are they complaining about? What do they do that seems unnecessarily hard? What do they buy to fix their problems? Don't ask them yet—just watch. Take notes. Notice patterns.

ai_config.reflection_prompt: What surprised you about people's frustrations? Was there a pattern across different people? Which problem seemed most real?

observation_config.briefing_text: Pick 3 people in your life. Could be a friend, a colleague, a family member, someone at your gym. Over the next week, observe them. What are they complaining about? What do they do that seems unnecessarily hard? What do they buy to fix their problems? Don't ask them yet—just watch. Take notes. Notice patterns.
guide_questions: What does this person complain about regularly?
What tasks do they avoid or procrastinate on?
What do they spend money on to solve problems?
What do they do that seems inefficient?
What makes them frustrated or stressed?

tasks.title: Add validated opportunities to your list
tasks.description: Look at your social observations. Which problems seemed most real? Which ones got people excited? Add them as opportunities.

metadata_config.source_context: Look at your social observations. Which problems seemed most real? Which ones got people excited? Add them as opportunities.

quest3.title: The World Out There
quest3.subtitle: Find problems that are big enough to build a business around
quest3.description: Now we're looking at the broader market. This is where you find problems that affect enough people to make a real business. You'll use tools like Google Trends, Reddit, Facebook Groups, and marketplaces to see what people are struggling with on a larger scale.
quest3.persona_prompt: You are helping the user map the landscape of problems. Guide them to look for patterns, not just individual complaints. Help them understand the difference between a niche problem and a market opportunity.

tasks.title: What are people searching for?
tasks.description: Open Google Trends. Search 5 terms related to problems you're curious about. Look at related queries—what are people searching for? Also check Reddit: what are people complaining about in subreddits related to your interests? This isn't about copying trends. It's about finding patterns of unmet need.

recommendations.title: How to Use Google Trends for Business Ideas
Reddit: The World's Largest Focus Group

ai_config.reflection_prompt: What surprised you in the search results? Was there a problem that seemed more common than you expected?

metadata_config.source_context: What did you find in Google Trends? What related queries came up? What seems to be a growing concern? Add them as opportunities.

tasks.title: Where do people talk about their problems?
tasks.description: Check Facebook Groups, LinkedIn communities, industry forums. Look for questions that keep coming up. Look for hacks and workarounds. If people are actively discussing a problem, it's worth paying attention to. Join the conversation—ask questions, not pitch.

recommendations.title: How to Ask Research Questions in Forums

ai_config.reflection_prompt: Which community had the most engaged discussions about problems? What does that tell you?

metadata_config.source_context: What problems did you find in forums? What questions keep coming up? Add them as opportunities.

tasks.title: What's already being sold?
tasks.description: Go to Amazon, Etsy, or wherever relevant. Search for products related to your problem area. What do people complain about in the reviews? 'I wish this had...' 'If only it could...' Those complaints are gold. They represent unmet needs that existing products aren't solving.

recommendations.title: Reading Between the Lines of Product Reviews

ai_config.reflection_prompt: What complaints kept coming up? Is there a gap in the market you could fill?

metadata_config.source_context: What complaints did you find in product reviews? What gaps did you identify? Add them as opportunities.

tasks.title: Consolidate your opportunity list
tasks.description: You've done a lot of research. You've got observations from yourself, from people you know, and from the broader market. Now it's time to review everything. Look at your list. Which problems seem most real? Which affect the most people? Which are you most excited to solve? Add the best ones to your master opportunity list.

recommendations.title: The Problem Filter: Separating Wheat from Chaff

quest4.title: Pick Your Path
quest4.subtitle: Validate, score, and commit to one opportunity
quest4.description: You've explored problems from every angle. You've looked inward, outward, and across the market. Now it's time to validate what's real, score your options, and commit to one. This is the moment of truth.
quest4.persona_prompt: You are helping the user make a clear decision. Don't let them waffle. Help them weigh the evidence, trust their gut, and commit. Remind them: they can always change direction later. The important thing is to start.

tasks.title: Validate your opportunities with real people
tasks.description: Take your top 5-10 opportunities. Go back to potential customers. Ask: 'Is this actually a problem for you? Would you pay for a solution?' This is the moment of truth. Log what you learn.

recommendations.title: How to Ask 'Would You Pay?' Without Being Pushy

ai_config.reflection_prompt: What did people say? Did anyone get genuinely excited? Did anyone tell you they'd pay? That's your signal.

tasks.title: Score your opportunities honestly
tasks.description:
Here's the truth: you can't pursue all of them. Let's get real. For each validated opportunity, score it honestly on these 5 criteria:

• **Do I actually care about this problem?** (1-10)
• **Do I know people who have this problem?** (1-10)
• **Could I talk to them easily?** (1-10)
• **Do I have any unfair advantage here?** (1-10)
• **Is there a clear way I could get paid?** (1-10)

recommendations.title: How to Choose the Right Business Idea
The 5 Tests of a Good Business Opportunity

ai_config.reflection_prompt: Looking at your scores, which opportunity stands out? Which one would you be most excited to tell people about?

tasks.title: Save your project
tasks.description: You've found it. The opportunity that passes the test. Save it as your project. This is your starting point. Everything from here on is about making this real. Congratulations—you've taken the hardest step.
